content: 1. Human fascioliasis is recognized as a significant public health issue, requiring a comprehensive approach to address its elimination. This includes advocacy to establish legal frameworks and intersectoral coordination, as well as agreement on technical plans for implementation across various sectors. 2. The acute phase of human fascioliasis presents with symptoms such as fever, gastrointestinal disturbances (nausea, vomiting, diarrhea), hepatomegaly, liver function abnormalities, skin rash, breathing difficulties, and abdominal pain or tenderness, often accompanied by high eosinophilia. 3. The chronic phase, occurring after the parasite settles in the bile ducts, is marked by inflammation, hyperplasia, and thickening of the bile ducts and gallbladder, potentially leading to lithiasis or biliary obstruction. Symptoms include biliary colic, nausea, intolerance to fatty foods, right upper quadrant pain, epigastric pain, obstructive jaundice, and pruritus. Liver and pancreatic inflammation may also occur. 4. Triclabendazole is the drug of choice for treating fascioliasis. It is effective against both adult parasites in the bile ducts and migrating juvenile parasites in the liver. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends a single oral dose of 10 mg/kg. In cases of therapeutic failure or when deemed necessary, two doses of 10 mg/kg can be administered 12–24 hours apart. 5. Monitoring the effectiveness of treatment involves microscopy 10–15 days post-treatment, with a follow-up at 30 days. Persistent positivity can be confirmed via ultrasound after 30–35 days. However, logistical challenges in remote areas may necessitate alternative approaches based on available resources. 6. Serological tests are not recommended for evaluating treatment effectiveness, as antibody levels remain elevated post-treatment, leading to continued positive results. 7. Therapeutic failure with triclabendazole is rare but has been reported. Potential causes include drug resistance, medication quality, dosage issues, or the patient’s immune status. Reinfection should also be ruled out in endemic areas. 8. Identifying at-risk populations is crucial before initiating public health programs. This involves assessing the endemicity of fascioliasis, the presence of intermediate host snails, and risk factors such as consumption of watercress or wild aquatic plants. 9. Preventive chemotherapy (PC) is recommended by WHO as a public health tool to treat infected individuals, prevent morbidity, and reduce transmission. PC can be implemented through mass drug administration, targeted chemotherapy, or selective chemotherapy based on infection prevalence and risk factors. 10. The drug of choice for PC is a single dose of 10 mg/kg of triclabendazole. Eligible populations include individuals aged 5–65 years in endemic areas, with some flexibility for younger children (4 years and above) and older adults in good health, based on local evidence and pharmacovigilance. 11. Pregnant or breastfeeding women, children under 4 years, individuals with acute gastrointestinal symptoms, and those with liver dysfunction should not receive PC but may be treated individually under medical supervision. 12. PC frequency depends on prevalence and modality, with annual administration suggested initially. Adjustments can be made based on impact surveys and progress toward eliminating fascioliasis as a public health problem. 13. Coordination with other preventive chemotherapy programs, such as soil-transmitted helminth control, is encouraged to optimize resources. However, simultaneous treatment for soil-transmitted helminths and fascioliasis is not recommended. 14. Adverse reactions to triclabendazole are generally mild, including abdominal pain, epigastric pain, and sweating. Less common reactions include nausea, vomiting, dizziness, cough, fever, urticaria, and pruritus. Monitoring adverse reactions during PC campaigns is essential. 15. Monitoring and evaluation are critical to assess the progress of elimination programs. This includes rapid assessments, baseline surveys, coverage analysis, sentinel site surveillance, and impact assessment surveys. 16. Rapid assessments in suspected endemic areas help determine the need for baseline population surveys. These assessments can be conducted in schools or communities, with at least 50 samples collected. Positive findings warrant a baseline survey. 17. Baseline surveys should use random probabilistic sampling to determine prevalence and infection intensity, focusing on school-age children (5–14 years) and adults if evidence suggests adult infections. 18. Monitoring PC coverage involves calculating the proportion of the target population that received treatment. Coverage analysis should be conducted after each PC round, with rapid monitoring in the first two weeks to address gaps and achieve optimal coverage (≥75%). 19. Strengthening technical capacities of intermediate laboratories in endemic areas is essential for conducting coprological tests and ensuring adequate sampling frequency. 20. Effective monitoring and evaluation plans are necessary to track progress toward eliminating human fascioliasis as a public health problem. These plans should include rapid assessments, baseline surveys, coverage monitoring, sentinel site surveillance, and impact assessment surveys.
